memory_verse.label: Bible Reference
memory_verse.text: Now Sarai, Abram's wife, had borne him no children. But she had an Egyptian slave named Hagar; so she said to Abram, "The Lord has kept me from having children. Go, sleep with my slave; perhaps I can build a family through her." - Gen 16:1-2 (NIV)

devotion.label: Devotion
devotion.text:
Ten years have passed since God's promise, and still no child. Sarai grows tired of waiting. So she devises a plan - a culturally acceptable one in her day - to obtain the promised child through her slave Hagar. On the surface it looks practical, even faithful. But underneath, it is an attempt to help God keep a promise He had not asked help with.

Notice her words: "The Lord has kept me from having children." She's not wrong that God had allowed her barrenness. But her conclusion is telling - since God hasn't acted, she will. She stops waiting on God and starts managing God's promise herself.

This is one of the most common failures of faith, and one of the most understandable. Waiting is hard. When God delays, we grow anxious, and anxiety pushes us to take matters into our own hands. We construct a workaround, tell ourselves it's just being sensible, and step out of God's timing into our own.

But God's promises are not projects for us to complete by our own scheming. They are gifts to be received in His time. Abram would learn, painfully, that "unless the Lord builds the house, the builders labor in vain" (Ps 127:1). Where are you tempted to "help God along" instead of trusting Him to keep His own word?

reflection.label: Reflection
reflection.text:
- Where are you tempted to force God's promise on your own timetable?
- Is impatience pushing you toward a workaround God never asked for?

prayer.label: Prayer
prayer.text:
Lord, forgive me for trying to help You keep Your promises through my own scheming. Teach me to wait on Your timing rather than forcing my own. Build my life Your way, not mine.
Amen.
